key_terms.meaning: φ = (actual fuel/air ratio) ÷ (stoichiometric fuel/air ratio); φ > 1 is rich, φ < 1 is lean, and it drives CO, HC and NOx together
The three-reaction chain N₂ + O → NO + N, N + O₂ → NO + O, N + OH → NO + H that makes most NO above about 1800 K
The thin gap between piston, rings and liner where flame cannot enter, so fuel hiding there leaves as unburnt HC
Flame dying out within about 1 mm of a cold wall, leaving a thin unburnt fuel layer behind
The part of diesel particulate that dissolves in solvent, made of unburnt lube oil and fuel, not carbon
A 0–10 scale read from the blackening of a filter paper by a fixed exhaust sample; it measures visible smoke, not total mass
A single catalyst that oxidises CO and HC while reducing NOx, but only inside a narrow window near φ = 1
EGR% = (mass of recirculated gas ÷ total charge mass) × 100; it dilutes the charge and lowers peak flame temperature
A platinum/palladium catalyst that oxidises CO, HC and the SOF of particles, and also makes NO₂ for the DPF and SCR
A wall-flow ceramic honeycomb that traps over 90% of particle mass and is cleaned by periodic regeneration above about 550 °C
Urea solution injected into the exhaust makes ammonia, which reacts with NOx on a vanadium or zeolite catalyst to give N₂ and water
A barium-based catalyst that stores NOx as nitrate during lean running and releases it for reduction during short rich pulses
Non-dispersive infrared instrument; CO absorbs strongly near 4.7 µm and CO₂ near 4.3 µm, so absorption gives concentration
A hydrogen flame burns the sample; carbon atoms ionise, the ion current is proportional to the number of carbon atoms, giving HC in ppmC
NO reacts with ozone to give excited NO₂, which emits light; the photon count is proportional to NO concentration
A fixed speed–time trace (for example the MIDC or WLTC) run on a chassis dynamometer so the work done is repeatable
Methane has a research octane number of about 120, so it resists knock and allows a higher compression ratio in an SI engine
Homogeneous charge compression ignition: a premixed lean charge ignited by compression heat alone, with no spark and no flame front
Reactivity controlled compression ignition: a low-reactivity fuel is port injected and a high-reactivity fuel is direct injected late to set ignition timing by fuel ratio
An optical method that turns refractive-index gradients into light and dark bands, showing density jumps such as sprays and flame fronts

takeaways: CO, unburnt HC and NOx each come from a different failure of combustion — too little oxygen, a flame that died or hid, and a flame that got too hot — so a single fix cannot remove all three.
Diesel particulate grows inside the rich core of the spray and then partly burns out later; smoke meters see only the black carbon part, not the whole mass.
In-cylinder methods stop the pollutant forming, after-treatment converts or traps it afterwards; modern engines need both together.
Each exhaust gas is measured by a physical effect unique to it: infrared absorption for CO and CO₂, ozone chemiluminescence for NO, a hydrogen flame for HC, filter blackening for smoke.
An emission standard is meaningless without its driving cycle, because the same engine gives different g/km on different speed traces.
An alternative fuel changes C/H ratio, octane or cetane number and storage difficulty at the same time, so all three must be traded together.
A dual-fuel engine uses a diesel pilot to light a gas that would not ignite on compression alone; a multi-fuel engine runs on one of several fuels at a time.
Low-temperature combustion avoids both NOx and soot by staying cool and lean, but the price is that ignition is set by chemical kinetics, not by spark or injection timing.
Optical engines and laser diagnostics turn a cylinder into a measuring cell and give the spatial detail that exhaust-gas analysis cannot.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on mechanism plus control: name the formation route, sketch the trade-off, then match it to a specific in-cylinder or after-treatment device and its limits.

bank.q: Explain how carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen are formed in a spark-ignition engine, and show that each comes from a different failure of the combustion process.
outline: CO: rich mixture or incomplete oxidation, water-gas shift frozen at exhaust, high at φ > 1
HC: crevice volumes, oil-film absorption, wall quenching, misfire, valve overlap short-circuiting
NOx: Zeldovich chain, needs local temperature above about 1800 K plus residence time and available oxygen
Effect of φ on all three: CO and HC rise rich of stoichiometric, NOx peaks slightly lean
Note that these are bulk trends and local in-cylinder conditions decide the actual values

bank.q: Describe the sequence by which a soot particle forms inside a diesel spray, and explain the difference between smoke, particulate mass and the soluble organic fraction.
outline: Liquid fuel breaks up into droplets; rich core with φ well above 1 and no oxygen
Pyrolysis to acetylene and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, then nucleation, surface growth, coagulation, agglomeration
Later mixing brings oxygen; part of the particle burns out, the rest leaves as exhaust particulate
Particulate mass = carbon + SOF + sulphate + ash; smoke is only the visible black carbon
Bosch smoke number or opacity measures light attenuation, so it misses the volatile part

bank.q: Classify emission control methods into in-cylinder treatments and after-treatment systems, and describe four devices of each class with their working principle.
outline: In-cylinder: EGR, retarded or optimised injection timing, high-pressure common rail and multiple injection, combustion chamber and port design, crankcase ventilation, precise air-fuel control
After-treatment: TWC, DOC, DPF, SCR, LNT
State the chemical reaction or trapping mechanism for each
Give the operating window and one failure mode for each device
Conclude that the two classes act at different points and are used together

bank.q: Explain the principle of operation of the NDIR analyser, the chemiluminescence NO analyser, the flame ionisation detector and a filter-type smoke meter.
outline: NDIR: broadband infrared source, gas cell, band-pass filter at the absorption band of the gas (4.7 µm CO, 4.3 µm CO₂), detector measures attenuation; Beer-Lambert relation
Chemiluminescence: NO + O₃ → NO₂* + O₂, photon emission proportional to NO; NO₂ must be converted to NO first for total NOx
FID: hydrogen flame, organic carbon ionises, ion current proportional to carbon count, response per carbon atom nearly equal, so ppmC
Smoke meter: fixed volume through filter paper, reflectance compared against a scale; gives Bosch number or opacity in %
State which gas is not handled by each method, for example NDIR cannot separate NO from NO₂ and FID does not see CO₂

bank.q: What is a driving cycle, and why is an emission standard defined as a cycle together with a limit rather than as a limit alone?
outline: Definition of a cycle: a fixed speed-time trace with defined gear changes and idling
Chassis dynamometer or engine dynamometer run, bag sampling and g/km or g/kWh result
Same vehicle gives different g/km for different traces: average speed, accelerations, idle fraction
Limits in g/km for light duty, g/kWh for heavy duty engines
Type approval versus in-service conformity and the role of the cycle in repeatability

bank.q: Distinguish a dual-fuel engine from a multi-fuel engine, and explain why the diesel pilot is needed in a gas dual-fuel engine.
outline: Dual fuel: two fuels present at the same time, gas is the main energy source, diesel is the pilot
Multi fuel: one fuel at a time selected from several; engine must cope with a wide cetane or octane range
Gas has a high octane number and low cetane number, so compression alone will not ignite it reliably in a diesel geometry
Pilot of about 5-10% diesel energy provides the ignition kernel
Discuss substitution ratio, knock limit at high gas fraction, and methane slip at light load

bank.q: An SI engine is set to run at φ = 1.05 with a three-way catalyst. Predict the raw CO, HC and NOx trends, the conversion efficiency of each gas, and state what you would change to bring the exhaust back into the catalyst window.
outline: Rich mixture: CO and HC rise sharply, NOx falls slightly from its lean peak
TWC window is roughly 0.99 < φ < 1.00, so CO and HC conversion stays high but NOx conversion drops steeply
Cause: insufficient oxygen to reduce NOx while oxidising CO and HC
Fixes: closed-loop oxygen sensor control, port fuel injection instead of carburettor, faster sensor, adaptive fuelling
Mention that the window must be held during transients, not only at steady state

bank.q: A diesel car must meet a strict NOx and particle number limit. Select an after-treatment layout and justify each element, explaining the role of fuel sulphur and exhaust temperature.
outline: Layout: DOC followed by DPF followed by SCR with urea dosing, or LNT for smaller vehicles
DOC: oxidises CO and HC, oxidises NO to NO₂ for passive DPF regeneration and fast SCR
DPF: wall-flow filtration, needs regeneration above about 550 °C or by NO₂ at 250-350 °C
SCR: urea to ammonia, standard reaction plus fast SCR route, ammonia slip control
Sulphur poisons catalysts and raises sulphate particulate, so low-sulphur fuel is a precondition; cold start and low load are the hard cases

bank.q: Compare CNG, hydrogen and biodiesel as SI and CI engine fuels using carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, octane or cetane number, energy density and storage. State the main engine change each one forces.
outline: CNG: mainly methane, high octane, low C/H, gas storage at 200 bar, needs spark ignition and a higher compression ratio
Hydrogen: no carbon, very high octane, wide flammability limits, very low density so storage is the problem; risk of backfire and pre-ignition, lubricity and NOx at high load
Biodiesel: high cetane, oxygenated, gives lower soot but higher NOx, cold-flow and oxidation stability issues, and it is not drop-in for all seals and materials
Energy density comparison per kg and per litre, and effect on vehicle range
Conclusion: performance, storage and emissions trade together, not separately

bank.q: An engine is to run in HCCI and then in RCCI mode. Describe the operating strategy, the control variable used to set ignition timing, and the expected emission behaviour in each case.
outline: HCCI: premixed lean charge, ignition by compression heat and chemical kinetics, no flame front
Control levers: intake temperature, EGR, compression ratio, fuel octane; all indirect and slow
Benefits: very low NOx and soot; problems: limited load range, ringing or knock at high load, high CO and HC, difficult cold start
RCCI: low-reactivity fuel port injected, high-reactivity fuel direct injected, ratio and timing set ignition
Higher load reach than HCCI with good control; still needs HC and CO oxidation after-treatment
Common requirement: low temperature combustion keeps peak temperature below the NOx threshold and φ low enough that soot cannot grow

bank.q: You must distinguish between fuel droplets, soot particles and NO inside a running diesel cylinder. Name an optical technique for each measurement and state what it actually detects and its main limitation.
outline: Droplets: Mie scattering or laser diffraction, detects elastic light scattered by the droplet surface, gives size and location but is sensitive to multiple scattering in dense spray
Soot: laser-induced incandescence, pulsed laser heats particles and the incandescence signal gives volume fraction, needs calibration
NO: laser-induced fluorescence, excites NO and detects fluorescence, quantitatively difficult because of quenching and tracer interference
Also mention Schlieren or shadowgraph for spray penetration and flame shape, and high-speed imaging
Optical access needs a transparent piston or liner, so geometry and wall temperature differ from the production engine

bank.q: Analyse the trade-off between NOx and soot in a direct-injection diesel engine, and explain how low-temperature combustion changes this relation.
outline: Conventional diffusion combustion has a rich core that makes soot and near-stoichiometric hot zones that make NOx
Advancing injection raises both; EGR and retarding cut NOx but tend to raise soot; the classic NOx-soot trade-off curve
Local temperature below about 1800 K stops the Zeldovich route; local φ below about 2 stops soot inception
LTC and RCCI create a dilute premixed charge that keeps both below the thresholds
Costs: ignition timing control, low-load CO and HC, combustion noise, limited load range, after-treatment for HC and CO still needed

bank.q: Evaluate whether a three-way catalytic converter alone can control emissions of a lean-burn gasoline engine, and discuss what alternatives exist.
outline: TWC needs simultaneous oxidising and reducing conditions, so it works only in a narrow band near stoichiometric
Lean exhaust carries excess oxygen, so NOx reduction is thermodynamically blocked and the catalyst saturates
Alternatives: LNT with periodic rich pulses, urea-based SCR on gasoline, and NOx storage plus on-board reformate
Penalty of rich pulses on fuel consumption; sulphur poisoning of the trap; durability and cost
Conclude that lean-burn gains in efficiency must pay for the extra after-treatment

bank.q: A city switches its buses from diesel to CNG and later tightens its standard to a Bharat Stage VI level. Evaluate the emission and practical consequences of each step, using formation chemistry, after-treatment needs and the driving cycle.
outline: CNG in a spark-ignition engine removes most soot and much of the CO and HC problem, but NOx remains and methane slip is a strong greenhouse gas
CNG also removes the DPF and its regeneration problems, and needs high-pressure storage and a refuelling network
BS VI level for diesel needs DOC plus DPF plus SCR with urea, low-sulphur fuel and on-board diagnostics
Cycle effect: a congested urban trace has more idle, cold start and low exhaust temperature, so catalyst light-off dominates the result
Overall judgement: fuel change and after-treatment are complementary, and the cycle decides whether the benefit shows up in g/km

bank.q: Explain how injection pressure, injection timing and multiple injection events change the fuel-air mixture history and hence CO, HC, NOx and smoke.
outline: Higher injection pressure means better atomisation, faster mixing, shorter rich duration, less soot
Retarded timing lowers peak temperature and NOx, but raises HC and CO and fuel consumption
Pilot injection reduces ignition delay and combustion noise; post injection supplies fuel for DPF regeneration or late oxidation of soot
Trade-off with wall wetting and oil dilution
Conclude that injection strategy is an in-cylinder emission control, not a power control only

glossary.def: A colourless, odourless, toxic gas formed when fuel carbon is only partly oxidised, mainly in rich or quenched regions.
Fuel or partly burnt fuel leaving the cylinder unchanged, from crevices, wall quenching, oil films, misfire or valve overlap.
Mainly NO with some NO₂, formed from atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen at high temperature inside the flame.
All solid and liquid material collected from diluted exhaust on a filter at a set temperature, including carbon, SOF, sulphate and ash.
The carbon-rich solid core of diesel particulate, formed by pyrolysis and growth of fuel molecules in an oxygen-poor zone.
The fraction of light blocked by an exhaust sample, expressed in percent; a fast but approximate smoke measure.
The air mass per unit fuel mass that exactly supplies the oxygen for complete combustion; about 14.7 for gasoline and 14.5 for diesel.
Returning part of the exhaust to the intake to dilute the charge and lower the peak combustion temperature, mainly to cut NOx.
A honeycomb coated with noble metal that speeds up oxidation or reduction reactions in the exhaust without being consumed.
Reduction of NOx to nitrogen and water by ammonia on a catalyst, used on lean exhaust where a TWC cannot work.
A 32.5% aqueous urea solution injected into the exhaust to make the ammonia that SCR needs.
A wall-flow filter that traps soot, cleaned by burning the collected carbon in a periodic regeneration event.
The burning off of soot stored in a DPF, either passively by NO₂ or actively by raising the exhaust temperature.
A catalyst that stores NOx during lean operation and reduces it during brief rich excursions.
O₃, used in the chemiluminescence analyser as the reagent that makes excited NO₂ emit light.
Parts per million of carbon atoms, the unit of the FID, which counts carbon rather than molecules.
A test bed with rollers under the driven wheels that applies road load so a driving cycle can be repeated indoors.
A scale of resistance to knock in a spark-ignition engine; higher means the fuel can stand a higher compression ratio.
A scale of ignition ease in a compression-ignition engine; higher means a shorter ignition delay.
A small early injection of high-cetane diesel used to ignite a main charge of gas or a low-reactivity fuel.
Any strategy that keeps local peak temperature below the NOx threshold and local equivalence ratio below the soot threshold.
The narrow gap region between piston crown and liner wall where flame quenches and leaves unburnt fuel.
A research engine with a transparent piston crown, liner or spacer so the combustion chamber can be photographed or laser-lit.
